notes.front: Under Regulation X, what is a referral?
notes.back: Any oral or written action directed at a person that affirmatively influences their choice of a settlement service provider, when they will pay for it.
notes.explanation: Because a referral is not a compensable service, paying for one is what section 8 forbids.
notes.example: Like a loan officer telling a buyer "use this title company, they are the best", where the buyer pays the title company's fees.
notes.evidence: A referral includes any oral or written action directed to a person which has the effect of affirmatively influencing the selection by any person of a provider of a settlement service

notes.front: What does the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit tell borrowers about predatory lending?
notes.back: To learn its warning signs, such as being told a loan is their "only chance" or that they must "act fast".
notes.explanation: The toolkit places this under what to do if you think you were a victim of a predatory lender or loan fraud.
notes.example: Like a caller who says the offer disappears tonight and no other lender will ever approve you, so sign now.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), I think I was a victim of a predatory lender or loan fraud, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Don’t believe anyone who tells you they are your “only chance to

notes.front: What is loan flipping, as Regulation Z restricts it for high-cost mortgages?
notes.back: Refinancing a high-cost mortgage into another high-cost mortgage for the same consumer within one year, unless it is in the consumer's interest.
notes.explanation: The rule binds the original creditor and any assignee holding or servicing the loan.
notes.example: Like a lender that refinances the same borrower every few months, charging fresh fees each time while the loan barely changes.
notes.evidence: Within one year of having extended a high-cost mortgage, a creditor shall not refinance any high-cost mortgage to the same consumer into another high-cost mortgage, unless the refinancing is in the consumer's interest.

notes.front: Under Regulation X, may anyone give or accept a fee or thing of value for referring settlement service business on a federally related mortgage loan?
notes.back: No. No person may give or accept it under any agreement or understanding, oral or otherwise.
notes.explanation: A referral of a settlement service is not a compensable service, with narrow exceptions.
notes.evidence: No person shall give and no person shall accept any fee, kickback or other thing of value pursuant to any agreement or understanding, oral or otherwise, that business incident to or part of a settlement service involving a federally related mortgage loan shall be referred to any person.

notes.front: A title agent gives a loan officer a $100 gift card for every client the officer sends. Is this allowed?
notes.back: No. It is a thing of value given for referrals, which section 8 of the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act forbids.
notes.explanation: A company may not pay another company or its employees for referring settlement service business.
notes.evidence: A company may not pay any other company or the employees of any other company for the referral of settlement service business.

notes.front: A lender never signed any referral deal with an appraisal firm, but gets a bonus each quarter tied to how many orders it sends. Can this still break the kickback ban?
notes.back: Yes. The agreement need not be written or spoken; a pattern can establish it, and payments tied to volume are evidence of one.
notes.explanation: Regulation X says repeated things of value connected to the volume of business referred are evidence of an agreement.
notes.evidence: An agreement or understanding for the referral of business incident to or part of a settlement service need not be written or verbalized but may be established by a practice, pattern or course of conduct.

notes.front: A lender pays its own loan officer a salary and a bonus for bringing in loans. Is that a forbidden referral fee?
notes.back: No. An employer's payment to its own employees for referral activities is permitted.
notes.explanation: Regulation X lists it among the payments section 8 permits.
notes.evidence: (vii) An employer's payment to its own employees for any referral activities.

notes.front: A title company runs a free seminar for estate agents on local tax changes, open to all and not tied to referrals. Is it allowed?
notes.back: Yes: normal promotional and educational activities not conditioned on referrals are permitted, if they do not pay costs the agents would otherwise bear.
notes.explanation: Regulation X permits such activity with those two conditions.
notes.evidence: Normal promotional and educational activities that are not conditioned on the referral of business and that do not involve the defraying of expenses that otherwise would be incurred by persons in a position to refer settlement services

notes.front: An estate agency and a mortgage broker agree to split fees on buyers they send each other. Does the cooperative brokerage exemption cover them?
notes.back: No. It covers fee divisions only between real estate agents and brokers acting as such, not with mortgage brokers.
notes.explanation: Regulation X says the exemption has no application to fee arrangements between real estate brokers and mortgage brokers.
notes.evidence: has no applicability to any fee arrangements between real estate brokers and mortgage brokers or between mortgage brokers.

notes.front: If a payment for goods or services bears no reasonable relationship to their market value, how does Regulation X treat the excess?
notes.back: The excess is not for services or goods actually performed or provided.
notes.explanation: This lets the Bureau look behind high prices for hidden referral fees.
notes.evidence: If the payment of a thing of value bears no reasonable relationship to the market value of the goods or services provided, then the excess is not for services or goods actually performed or provided.

notes.front: A lender requires a borrower to use its chosen settlement company, which the borrower pays. Has a referral occurred?
notes.back: Yes. Requiring a person who pays for a settlement service to use a particular provider is a referral.
notes.explanation: Regulation X treats required use as a referral in its own right.
notes.evidence: A referral also occurs whenever a person paying for a settlement service or business incident thereto is required to use (see § 1024.2, “required use”) a particular provider of a settlement service

notes.front: Is making a referral of a settlement service a compensable service in itself?
notes.back: No, except as Regulation X allows (such as employers paying their own employees).
notes.explanation: So a fee for "referral services" is not saved by calling it a service.
notes.evidence: Any referral of a settlement service is not a compensable service, except as set forth in § 1024.14(g)(1).

notes.front: May a settlement service provider share part of a charge with someone who performed no services?
notes.back: No. No one may give or accept a split of a settlement charge other than for services actually performed.
notes.explanation: Regulation X calls a charge for no or nominal services an unearned fee.
notes.evidence: No person shall give and no person shall accept any portion, split, or percentage of any charge made or received for the rendering of a settlement service in connection with a transaction involving a federally related mortgage loan other than for services actually performed.

notes.front: A broker adds a $300 "document review" fee to a closing but does no real work for it. How does Regulation X classify the fee?
notes.back: As an unearned fee, which violates the rule.
notes.explanation: A charge for which no or nominal services are performed, or which duplicates another fee, is unearned.
notes.evidence: A charge by a person for which no or nominal services are performed or for which duplicative fees are charged is an unearned fee and violates this section.

notes.front: Does it matter who pays a charge when deciding whether the service is compensable?
notes.back: No. The source of the payment does not determine whether a service is compensable.
notes.explanation: Nor can the ban be avoided by having the purchaser split the fee.
notes.evidence: The source of the payment does not determine whether or not a service is compensable.

notes.front: What does Regulation Z forbid a covered person to do about the value assigned to a consumer's principal dwelling?
notes.back: Cause or try to cause it to be based on anything other than the appraiser's independent judgment, through coercion, bribery and similar means.
notes.explanation: The ban covers direct and indirect attempts.
notes.evidence: no covered person shall or shall attempt to directly or indirectly cause the value assigned to the consumer's principal dwelling to be based on any factor other than the independent judgment of a person that prepares valuations

notes.front: A loan officer emails the appraiser: "We need at least $410,000 for this deal to work." Which prohibited act is this?
notes.back: Seeking to influence the appraiser to report a minimum value.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z gives this as its first example of coercion.
notes.evidence: Seeking to influence a person that prepares a valuation to report a minimum or maximum value for the consumer's principal dwelling;

notes.front: A lender tells an appraiser it will pay the invoice only if the value comes in at or above the contract price. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. Withholding or threatening to withhold timely payment because of the value is coercion.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z still permits withholding pay for breach of contract or substandard work.
notes.evidence: Withholding or threatening to withhold timely payment to a person that prepares a valuation or performs valuation management functions because the person does not value the consumer's principal dwelling at or above a certain amount;

notes.front: A broker drops an appraiser from its panel because her last value fell short of the sale price. What does Regulation Z say?
notes.back: That excluding an appraiser from future work because a value missed a predetermined threshold is coercion.
notes.explanation: Implying that future retention depends on the value is also listed.
notes.evidence: Excluding a person that prepares a valuation from consideration for future engagement because the person reports a value for the consumer's principal dwelling that does not meet or exceed a predetermined threshold;

notes.front: An appraisal firm is paid only if the loan closes. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. Conditioning the appraiser's pay on consummation of the transaction is prohibited.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z lists it among the examples of coercion.
notes.evidence: Conditioning the compensation paid to a person that prepares a valuation on consummation of the covered transaction.

notes.front: The appraiser assigned to a home is the seller's cousin and stands to share in the sale proceeds. May she appraise it?
notes.back: No. A person preparing a valuation may have no direct or indirect interest, financial or otherwise, in the property or transaction.
notes.explanation: This is Regulation Z's conflict-of-interest rule for valuations.
notes.evidence: No person preparing a valuation or performing valuation management functions for a covered transaction may have a direct or indirect interest, financial or otherwise, in the property or transaction for which the valuation is or will be performed.

notes.front: What is the general anti-discrimination rule in Regulation B?
notes.back: A creditor must not discriminate against an applicant on a prohibited basis regarding any aspect of a credit transaction.
notes.explanation: The comment says it covers all dealings between applicant and creditor, whether or not other provisions address them.
notes.evidence: A creditor shall not discriminate against an applicant on a prohibited basis regarding any aspect of a credit transaction.

notes.front: A loan officer shows only high-priced "subprime" products to minority callers but a full range to similar non-minority callers. What is this?
notes.back: Disparate treatment on a prohibited basis.
notes.explanation: Regulation B's commentary uses this very pattern as an example.
notes.evidence: A creditor provides information only on “subprime” and similar products to minority applicants who request information about the creditor's mortgage products, but provides information on a wider variety of mortgage products to similarly situated nonminority applicants.

notes.front: An underwriter asks a minority applicant for two extra years of bank statements not asked of a similar non-minority applicant. What is this?
notes.back: Disparate treatment: requiring greater documentation on a prohibited basis.
notes.explanation: It is one of Regulation B's listed examples.
notes.evidence: A creditor requires a minority applicant to provide greater documentation to obtain a loan than a similarly situated nonminority applicant.

notes.front: A manager overlooks a late payment for a non-minority applicant but not for a similar minority applicant. What is this?
notes.back: Disparate treatment: waiving or relaxing credit standards for one group only.
notes.explanation: It is one of Regulation B's listed examples.
notes.evidence: A creditor waives or relaxes credit standards for a nonminority applicant but not for a similarly situated minority applicant.

notes.front: A loan officer explains every product in detail to men but gives women a short brochure. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. Giving more comprehensive information to men than to similarly situated women is disparate treatment.
notes.explanation: Regulation B lists this example.
notes.evidence: A creditor provides more comprehensive information to men than to similarly situated women.

notes.front: An advert implies that applicants from a certain religion will be offered worse terms. Which Regulation B rule is broken, even if no one applies?
notes.back: The ban on discouragement: statements that would lead a reasonable person to expect denial or worse terms on a prohibited basis.
notes.explanation: The rule covers statements to prospective applicants, in advertising or otherwise.
notes.evidence: A creditor shall not make any oral or written statement, in advertising or otherwise, directed at applicants or prospective applicants that the creditor knows or should know would cause a reasonable person to believe that the creditor would deny, or would grant on less favorable terms

notes.front: When is treating applicants differently on a prohibited basis unlawful?
notes.back: When the creditor lacks a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason, or its stated reason is a pretext.
notes.explanation: Regulation B's commentary states both conditions.
notes.evidence: Treating applicants differently on a prohibited basis is unlawful if the creditor lacks a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason for its action, or if the asserted reason is found to be a pretext for discrimination.

notes.front: The driving licence an applicant gives shows signs of alteration. What does the Red Flags Rule guidance call this?
notes.back: A red flag: documents provided for identification appear altered or forged.
notes.explanation: The guidance lists suspicious documents among its examples of red flags.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Identity Theft Rules), 1 January 2026 edition, Supplement A to Appendix A, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: appear to have been altered or forged

notes.front: The photograph on an applicant's identification does not match the person at the desk. Is this a red flag?
notes.back: Yes. A photograph or description on the identification that does not match the person presenting it is a listed red flag.
notes.explanation: It falls under suspicious documents in the guidance.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Identity Theft Rules), 1 January 2026 edition, Supplement A to Appendix A, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: on the identification is not consistent with

notes.front: An applicant's Social Security number matches one already used by another customer. What should the loan officer recognise?
notes.back: A red flag: a Social Security number the same as one submitted by others.
notes.explanation: The guidance lists it under suspicious personal identifying information.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Identity Theft Rules), 1 January 2026 edition, Supplement A to Appendix A, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: provided is the same as that

notes.front: The home address on an application turns out to be a mail drop. Is that a red flag?
notes.back: Yes. An application address that is fictitious, a mail drop or a prison is a listed red flag.
notes.explanation: It falls under suspicious personal identifying information.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Identity Theft Rules), 1 January 2026 edition, Supplement A to Appendix A, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: the address on an application is

notes.front: What must a loan or finance company file with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network?
notes.back: A report of any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation.
notes.explanation: The report is filed as a suspicious activity report.
notes.source: 31 CFR part 1029, 1 July 2025 edition, § 1029.320(a)(1), PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: a report of any suspicious

notes.front: What dollar amount must a suspicious transaction involve, alone or in aggregate, for a loan company to have to report it?
notes.back: At least $5,000 in funds or other assets.
notes.explanation: Below that, the company may still file voluntarily.
notes.source: 31 CFR part 1029, 1 July 2025 edition, § 1029.320(a)(2), PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: funds or other assets of at least

notes.front: A lender detects facts on 1 May that may justify a SAR and has identified the suspect. By when must it file?
notes.back: No later than 30 calendar days after initial detection (by 31 May).
notes.explanation: The extra 30 days apply only when no suspect has been identified, and never beyond 60 days in total.
notes.source: 31 CFR part 1029, 1 July 2025 edition, § 1029.320(b)(3), PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: no later than 30 calendar days after the

notes.front: If no suspect is identified on the date of initial detection, how long may a loan company delay filing a SAR?
notes.back: An additional 30 calendar days, but never more than 60 days after initial detection.
notes.explanation: The delay is allowed only to identify a suspect.
notes.source: 31 CFR part 1029, 1 July 2025 edition, § 1029.320(b)(3), PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: may delay filing a SAR for an

notes.front: A flyer says "No fees, ever!" but the loan carries a $1,200 origination fee. Which misrepresentation is this under the advertising rule?
notes.back: A misrepresentation about the existence, nature or amount of fees or costs to the consumer.
notes.explanation: Fees and costs are one of the listed subjects of prohibited misrepresentations.
notes.source: 12 CFR part 1014 (Regulation N), 1 January 2026 edition, § 1014.3, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: of fees or costs to the consumer

notes.front: A mailer carries an eagle and the words "Federal Housing Relief Notice" though the lender has no government link. What does the advertising rule say?
notes.back: It prohibits misrepresenting any association of the product or provider with a governmental entity.
notes.explanation: Association with government bodies is one of the listed subjects.
notes.source: 12 CFR part 1014 (Regulation N), 1 January 2026 edition, § 1014.3, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: credit product or any provider of such

notes.front: An advert compares a two-year introductory payment with a competitor's full-term payment without saying the intro payment ends. What does the rule target?
notes.back: Misleading comparisons between a rate or payment available for less than the full term and another rate or payment.
notes.explanation: Such comparisons are a listed subject of misrepresentation.
notes.source: 12 CFR part 1014 (Regulation N), 1 January 2026 edition, § 1014.3, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: available for a period less than the full

notes.front: According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ARM handbook, what should an ARM advert that shows an initial rate also show?
notes.back: How long the initial rate is in effect, and the annual percentage rate.
notes.explanation: If the annual percentage rate is much higher than the initial rate, payments may rise a lot after the introductory period.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 6.3 Advertisements, PDF p. 31
notes.evidence: Any ad for an ARM that shows an initial interest rate should also show how long the rate is in eﬀect and the APR on the loan.

notes.front: Which federal law does the 2006 nontraditional guidance cite as prohibiting unfair or deceptive acts or practices?
notes.back: Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act.
notes.explanation: The guidance adds that state laws on unfair or deceptive practices may also apply.
notes.source: Interagency Guidance on Nontraditional Mortgage Product Risks, 71 FR 58609 (4 October 2006), Communications with Consumers, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Act prohibits unfair or deceptive

notes.front: What does the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit say about quoting low fees on the Loan Estimate and then charging much more?
notes.back: It is illegal to quote low fees and costs and then surprise the borrower with much higher costs later.
notes.explanation: A lender may change fees only for reasons such as changed facts, a borrower's request or an expired estimate.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 2. Review your revised Loan Estimate, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: It is illegal for a lender to quote you low fees and costs for its services on your Loan Estimate and then surprise you with much higher costs in a revised Loan Estimate or Closing Disclosure.

notes.front: A lender raises its quoted fees because the borrower asked to switch loan programmes. Is that allowed?
notes.back: Yes. A lender may change quoted fees when the borrower asks for a change.
notes.explanation: The toolkit also lists wrong or changed facts, not qualifying for the original offer, and an expired estimate.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 2. Review your revised Loan Estimate, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: However, a lender is allowed to change the fees it quotes you for its services if the facts on your application were wrong or changed, you asked for a change

notes.front: A lender tells a hesitant borrower, "Sign today or lose this deal: no one else will lend to you." What should the borrower recognise?
notes.back: Warning signs of predatory lending: "only chance" and "act fast" pressure.
notes.explanation: The toolkit tells borrowers not to believe such claims.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), I think I was a victim of a predatory lender or loan fraud, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Learn the warning signs of predatory lending and protect yourself.

notes.front: Before closing a high-cost refinance, a broker tells the borrower to stop paying the old loan. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. A creditor or broker may not recommend or encourage default on an existing loan being refinanced into a high-cost mortgage.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z lists this among the practices barred for high-cost mortgages.
notes.evidence: may not recommend or encourage default on an existing loan or other debt prior to and in connection with the consummation or account opening of a high-cost mortgage

notes.front: May a creditor finance the points and fees on a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: No. Charges that count as points and fees may not be financed.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z lists this among the high-cost mortgage prohibitions.
notes.evidence: A creditor that extends credit under a high-cost mortgage may not finance charges that are required to be included in the calculation of points and fees

notes.front: Eight months after a high-cost loan, the creditor refinances it into another, relying only on the borrower signing "this loan is in my interest". Is that enough?
notes.back: No. A written statement alone does not meet the standard; interest is judged on the totality of the circumstances.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z's comment rejects a bare statement.
notes.evidence: A written statement by the borrower that “this loan is in my interest” alone does not meet this standard.

notes.front: Four months after a high-cost loan, a borrower needs funds for a bona fide personal financial emergency and the creditor refinances. Can this be in the borrower's interest?
notes.back: Yes. A refinance needed to meet a bona fide personal financial emergency would be in the borrower's interest.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z's comment gives this example.
notes.evidence: A refinancing would be in the borrower's interest if needed to meet the borrower's “bona fide personal financial emergency”

notes.front: Can a creditor avoid the one-year refinancing ban by arranging for other creditors to refinance its high-cost loans?
notes.back: No. Acts or practices to evade the rule are prohibited, including a pattern of arranging refinancings through affiliated or unaffiliated creditors.
notes.explanation: The ban also covers assignees holding or servicing the loan.
notes.evidence: A creditor (or assignee) is prohibited from engaging in acts or practices to evade this provision, including a pattern or practice of arranging for the refinancing of its own loans by affiliated or unaffiliated creditors.

notes.front: When is a loan originator barred from directing a consumer to a loan?
notes.back: When the reason is that the originator earns more on it than on other loans offered, unless the loan is in the consumer's interest.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z calls this steering.
notes.evidence: a loan originator shall not direct or “steer” a consumer to consummate a transaction based on the fact that the originator will receive greater compensation from the creditor in that transaction than in other transactions the originator offered or could have offered to the consumer, unless the consummated transaction is in the consumer's interest.

notes.front: For the steering safe harbour, which three loan options must be presented for each type of transaction?
notes.back: The lowest rate; the lowest rate without risky features; and the lowest total points, origination points or fees.
notes.explanation: Presenting these is deemed to comply with the anti-steering rule.
notes.evidence: The loan with the lowest interest rate;

notes.front: For the safe harbour, the originator presents a loan with a balloon payment in year 5 as the "lowest rate without risky features". Does that work?
notes.back: No. That option must exclude, among others, a balloon payment in the first 7 years.
notes.explanation: The option also excludes negative amortisation, prepayment penalties and interest-only payments.
notes.evidence: The loan with the lowest interest rate without negative amortization, a prepayment penalty, interest-only payments, a balloon payment in the first 7 years of the life of the loan

notes.front: A broker regularly works with five creditors. How many must it obtain options from to use the steering safe harbour?
notes.back: A significant number: three or more of them.
notes.explanation: If it worked with fewer than three, options from all of them would suffice.
notes.evidence: A significant number of the creditors with which a loan originator regularly does business is three or more of those creditors.

notes.front: Two loans suit a borrower equally; the officer pushes the one paying him a larger commission and it costs the borrower more. What has happened?
notes.back: Steering: directing the consumer to a loan because it pays the originator more, not because it is in the consumer's interest.
notes.explanation: The rule allows the higher-paying loan only if it is in the consumer's interest.
notes.evidence: unless the consummated transaction is in the consumer's interest.

notes.front: Where does the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit tell borrowers to submit a complaint about problems during the application or closing?
notes.back: To the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
notes.explanation: The toolkit says this applies at any stage, and later if there are payment problems.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), I have a complaint, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Submit a complaint to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau if you have problems at any stage of the mortgage application or closing process

notes.front: After the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau forwards a consumer complaint to a company, how long does the company have to respond?
notes.back: 15 days.
notes.explanation: The consumer can then review the response and give feedback.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), Appendix B: More information, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: Companies have 15 days to respond to you and the CFPB.

notes.front: What is one thing Regulation Z's commentary says may be evidence that an ability-to-repay decision was not in good faith?
notes.back: For example, the creditor disregarded evidence that the consumer may have too little residual income.
notes.explanation: Other examples include early default and applying underwriting standards inconsistently.
notes.evidence: The creditor disregarded evidence that the consumer may have insufficient residual income to cover other recurring obligations and expenses

notes.front: Underwriting shows a borrower can repay only if she later refinances or sells. The creditor approves anyway. What does the commentary say?
notes.back: Disregarding evidence that the consumer could repay only by refinancing or selling may show the decision was not reasonable or in good faith.
notes.explanation: The commentary lists it among signs of an unreasonable determination.
notes.evidence: The creditor disregarded evidence that the consumer would have the ability to repay only if the consumer subsequently refinanced the loan or sold the property securing the loan.

notes.front: A creditor relaxes its usual underwriting standards for one borrower without any reasonable justification. What might this suggest?
notes.back: That its ability-to-repay determination was not reasonable or in good faith.
notes.explanation: Applying standards inconsistently without justification is listed as possible evidence.
notes.evidence: The creditor applied underwriting standards inconsistently or used underwriting standards different from those used for similar loans without reasonable justification;

notes.front: According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau toolkit, who is responsible for an accurate and truthful loan application?
notes.back: The borrower, who should be upfront; mortgage fraud is a serious offence.
notes.explanation: The toolkit's list of pitfalls warns against fudging numbers or documents.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 8. Avoid pitfalls, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: You are responsible for an accurate and truthful application. Be upfront

notes.front: A borrower asks the loan officer to leave a recent collection account off the application. What does the toolkit say about hiding such information?
notes.back: Don't hide important financial information: hiding negative information might delay or derail the application.
notes.explanation: The borrower is responsible for a truthful application.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 8. Avoid pitfalls, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Hiding negative information might delay or derail your loan application.

notes.front: For a loan originator's qualification, how long does a felony involving fraud, dishonesty, breach of trust or money laundering count against them?
notes.back: At any time, not only within the preceding seven years.
notes.explanation: Other felonies count if within the preceding seven-year period.
notes.evidence: in the case of a felony involving an act of fraud, dishonesty, a breach of trust, or money laundering, at any time;

notes.front: At signing, a borrower notices blank spaces in a loan document and the officer says "we'll fill those in later". What does the toolkit advise?
notes.back: Don't sign documents where important details are left blank.
notes.explanation: The toolkit ties this to protecting yourself from fraud.
notes.source: Your home loan toolkit (CFPB), 8. Avoid pitfalls, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Don’t sign documents where

notes.front: Must a mortgage broker find a borrower the best deal?
notes.back: Not unless it has contracted to act as the borrower's agent, or state law gives it that duty.
notes.explanation: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau handbook notes brokers generally contact several lenders to find one.
notes.source: Consumer Handbook on Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (CFPB, 2014), 2. What is an ARM?, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: brokers are not required to find the best deal for you unless they have contracted with you to act as your agent, or have a duty to do so under state law.

notes.front: A loan officer refers a borrower to a title company the officer's employer part-owns. What must the written disclosure explain?
notes.back: The nature of the relationship, including the ownership and financial interest, and an estimate of the provider's charges.
notes.explanation: This is the affiliated business arrangement disclosure.
notes.evidence: of the nature of the relationship (explaining the ownership and financial interest) between the provider of settlement services (or business incident thereto) and the person making the referral and of an estimated charge or range of charges generally made by such provider

notes.front: Under the Safeguards Rule, who must oversee a financial institution's information security programme?
notes.back: A designated qualified individual.
notes.explanation: That person may be employed by the institution, an affiliate or a service provider.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 1 January 2026 edition, § 314.4(a), PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Designate a qualified individual

notes.front: Under the Safeguards Rule, when must customer information be encrypted?
notes.back: Both in transit over external networks and at rest.
notes.explanation: If encryption is infeasible, approved compensating controls may be used instead.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 1 January 2026 edition, § 314.4(c)(3), PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: by you both in transit over external

notes.front: A mortgage company's marketing staff can open every file of borrower tax returns. What does the Safeguards Rule require?
notes.back: Limit authorised users' access to only the customer information they need to perform their duties.
notes.explanation: Access controls are part of the required safeguards.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 1 January 2026 edition, § 314.4(c)(1)(ii), PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: (ii) Limit authorized users’ access

notes.front: A home-improvement firm asks a lender for a list of its recent borrowers' names and loan amounts. Under Regulation P, what must happen first?
notes.back: Each consumer must have had the initial and opt-out notices and a reasonable chance to opt out, and not opted out.
notes.explanation: Nonpublic personal information may not go to a nonaffiliated third party without those steps, except as otherwise authorised.
notes.evidence: you may not, directly or through any affiliate, disclose any nonpublic personal information about a consumer to a nonaffiliated third party unless:

notes.front: A borrower returned the opt-out form. May the lender now share her nonpublic personal information with a nonaffiliated marketer?
notes.back: No. Disclosure is allowed only if the consumer does not opt out (other exceptions aside).
notes.explanation: Not opting out is the last of Regulation P's conditions.
notes.evidence: (iv) The consumer does not opt out.
